notes: Questions are written as conversational Biblical moments; Episode 10 free/paid hints guide thinking, with optional letter reveal separate. Answers, IDs, rewards and source references unchanged.

g10-d01.clue: Abraham's life ends, but Jehovah's promise doesn't. Which son does Genesis say Jehovah continued to bless?
g10-d01.explanation: Abraham dies at 175, and Isaac and Ishmael bury him. Then Genesis 25:11 gives us this comforting detail: Jehovah continues to bless Isaac. The promise hasn't ended with Abraham's death.
g10-d01.hint1: Remember, Abraham's two sons came together to bury him. The promise continued through one of them.
g10-d01.hint2: Think of the son Sarah gave birth to when she and Abraham were already old.
g10-d01.hint3: He married Rebekah, and their sons later became known as Jacob and Esau.

g10-d02.clue: Rebekah felt a struggle inside her before the birth. What was she expecting when she asked Jehovah about it?
g10-d02.explanation: Rebekah asked Jehovah why her pregnancy was so difficult. His answer went far beyond the birth itself: the two boys would become two peoples. Then Esau and Jacob were born. (Genesis 25:22–26)
g10-d02.hint1: Jehovah didn't just tell her about one child. He spoke about two peoples who would come from her.
g10-d02.hint2: The account describes a pair of boys sharing the same pregnancy.
g10-d02.hint3: Esau was born first. Jacob followed, holding Esau's heel.

g10-d03.clue: Jacob was known for living in tents, but Esau loved life out in the field. What did Esau become skilled at?
g10-d03.explanation: Genesis 25:27 draws a vivid contrast: Esau became a skilled hunter, while Jacob was described as a blameless man dwelling in tents. They grew up together, but their lives took different directions.
g10-d03.hint1: Genesis describes two brothers with very different daily lives. Jacob stayed around the tents.
g10-d03.hint2: Esau's skill took him out into the open country, where he searched for wild game.
g10-d03.hint3: Picture someone tracking an animal with a bow and arrows, hoping to bring food home.

g10-d04.clue: Can you imagine trading something precious for one meal? What simple food did Esau receive when he gave up his birthright?
g10-d04.explanation: Esau was exhausted when he came in from the field. He agreed to sell his birthright and ate bread and lentil stew. Genesis 25:34 says he despised the birthright. That one meal came at a terrible price.
g10-d04.hint1: The meal looked small compared with what Esau was giving up.
g10-d04.hint2: It was a reddish stew served with bread, made from a plant rather than meat.
g10-d04.hint3: Genesis 25:34 names the little legumes in Jacob's stew. They're often used in soups.

g10-d05.clue: A famine could have sent Isaac toward Egypt. Where did he remain when Jehovah told him not to go there?
g10-d05.explanation: During the famine, Jehovah told Isaac not to go down to Egypt. Isaac remained in Gerar, and Jehovah repeated the promise he had made to Abraham. (Genesis 26:1–6)
g10-d05.hint1: This happened in the region ruled by a Philistine king.
g10-d05.hint2: The king was named Abimelech, and Isaac stayed in his territory.
g10-d05.hint3: Genesis 26:6 names the town. It's also where Isaac later faced problems over wells.

g10-d06.clue: After people argued over Isaac's first wells, he finally found one where nobody fought him. What did he call it?
g10-d06.explanation: Isaac had moved from well to well because of arguments over water. At last there was no quarrel. He named that well Rehoboth and spoke about Jehovah making room for them. (Genesis 26:22)
g10-d06.hint1: The earlier names Esek and Sitnah were connected with disputes. This well was different.
g10-d06.hint2: Isaac said Jehovah had made room for his household.
g10-d06.hint3: The name in Genesis 26:22 is connected with having enough space to spread out.

g10-d07.clue: After so much tension over land and water, Isaac and Abimelech finally make peace. What do they swear to each other?
g10-d07.explanation: Abimelech and his companions came to Isaac because they could see Jehovah was with him. They agreed to live in peace, shared a meal, and swore an oath the next morning. (Genesis 26:26–31)
g10-d07.hint1: It wasn't merely a friendly goodbye. They made a serious agreement.
g10-d07.hint2: Both sides promised not to harm one another.
g10-d07.hint3: Genesis 26:31 describes a solemn pledge they swore to each other.

g10-d08.clue: Isaac couldn't see well, and Jacob worried that his smooth skin would give him away. What did Rebekah put on his hands?
g10-d08.explanation: Rebekah used the skins of young goats to cover Jacob's hands and the smooth part of his neck. The account shows how far the deception went. (Genesis 27:14–17)
g10-d08.hint1: Jacob knew his father might feel his skin and discover the disguise.
g10-d08.hint2: The material was taken from young animals used to prepare the meal.
g10-d08.hint3: Rebekah covered Jacob's hands and neck with their hairy skins. (Genesis 27:16)

g10-d09.clue: Esau returned to his father and found that Jacob had already received something meant for him. What was it?
g10-d09.explanation: Jacob approached Isaac pretending to be Esau and received his father's blessing. When Esau arrived later, he was deeply upset. Genesis doesn't hide the pain this caused the family. (Genesis 27:18–38)
g10-d09.hint1: It wasn't an animal, a meal, or a piece of land.
g10-d09.hint2: Isaac had spoken words about Jacob's future and Jehovah's favor.
g10-d09.hint3: Esau cried out when he realized he hadn't received what his father had intended for him.

g10-d10.clue: Jacob was sleeping outdoors when Jehovah reassured him through a remarkable dream. What did he name that place afterward?
g10-d10.explanation: On the way toward Haran, Jacob dreamed of a stairway and heard Jehovah's promises. When he woke, he set up the stone and named that place Bethel. (Genesis 28:10–22)
g10-d10.hint1: The name came after Jacob woke up and set up the stone he had used.
g10-d10.hint2: He recognized the place as connected with Jehovah's presence.
g10-d10.hint3: The name means 'House of God.' Genesis 28:19 gives it.
